title: What Does It Mean to Be White?
abstract: does it mean to be white in a society that proclaims race meaningless yet is deeply divided by race? In the face of pervasive racial inequality and segregation, most whites cannot answer that question. Robin DiAngelo argues that a number of factors make this question difficult for whites miseducation about what racism is; ideologies such as individualism and colorblindness; defensiveness; and a need to protect (rather than expand) our worldviews. These factors contribute to what she terms white racial illiteracy. Speaking as a white person to other white people, Dr. DiAngelo clearly and compellingly takes readers through an analysis of white socialization. She describes how race shapes the lives of white people, explains what makes racism so hard for whites to see, identifies common white racial patterns, and speaks back to popular white narratives that work to deny racism. Written as an accessible introduction to white identity from an anti-racist framework, What Does It Mean To Be White? is an invaluable resource for members of diversity and anti-racism programs and study groups and students of sociology, psychology, education, and other disciplines.

narrative:
Short impact summary

Robin DiAngelo's 2016 scholarly book What Does It Mean to Be White? has established itself as a foundational reference in critical race theory and education research. With 130 citations and placement in the top 10% of works by citation impact in its field and year, the book has shaped academic discourse on racial identity, whiteness, and pedagogy across education, teacher training, and social psychology. Its reach extends internationally, particularly across North America, Northern Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region.

Full narrative

Published by Peter Lang Verlag as part of the Counterpoints series, DiAngelo's work addresses a fundamental question often avoided in predominantly white contexts: what does whiteness mean in societies that simultaneously deny race's significance while remaining structurally divided by it? The book argues that white individuals struggle to answer this question due to miseducation about racism, ideologies of individualism and colorblindness, defensive reactions, and resistance to worldview expansion. This framing has proven influential in reshaping how educators, scholars, and practitioners conceptualize racial identity development and anti-racist pedagogy.

The citation landscape reveals concentrated uptake within educational contexts, with 85 of 130 citing works located in the education sector. Critical race theory in education emerges as the dominant conceptual framework for citing works, appearing in 46 publications, followed by teacher education and leadership studies (20 works), and educator training and historical pedagogy (15 works). This distribution underscores the book's particular salience for those training educators and developing curriculum. Twenty dissertations have cited the work, indicating its adoption as a reference point in graduate-level research on racial pedagogy, identity, and teacher preparation.

Citation momentum accelerated notably after publication, with annual citations rising from 10 in 2016 to a peak of 22 in 2019, demonstrating sustained and growing engagement. The work has also gained traction across multiple English-speaking regions—the United States accounts for 68 citations, while Canada (6), Sweden (5), New Zealand (4), and Australia (3) show meaningful adoption. Beyond education, the book has resonated in healthcare (7 citations) and nonprofit sectors (3 citations), reflecting broader organizational interest in racial awareness and anti-racist practice.

Recent citing works through 2025 continue to draw on DiAngelo's framework, with titles addressing racial socialization across the life course, Asian American experiences in medicine, and linguistic discrimination in early childhood settings demonstrating its application across diverse contexts. The book is catalogued in multiple institutional library systems and has sustained scholarly circulation, establishing it as a key text in conversations about white identity, structural racism, and educational justice.
